Decolonizing time: Chicana femme decolonial aesthetics and ancient serpent temporalities

Alejandra I. Ramírez

The serpent has become a symbol systematically corrupted by colonial chronobiopolitics, but it reemerges in Chicana femme art as a symbol of decolonial time. This article examines how select artworks of Amalia Mesa-Bains, Diane Gamboa, and Anel Flores mobilize serpentine aesthetics as embodied rhetorical practices that dismantle linear temporality. Networked perversion: fascism, misogyny, and the man versus bear meme

M. Aubrey Studebaker; Meredith Neville-Shepard

Misogynists have smugly scoffed and projected outrage at women who suggest that, if trapped alone in the woods, they would feel safer encountering a bear than a man. Through an analysis of anti-feminist engagement in the Man versus Bear meme on X, we explore cultural misogyny online as a mode of networked perversity that rehearses a fascist social order. Hunting monsters: postracial fantasies in the third golden age of horror

Kendall R. Phillips

This essay extends Eric King Watts’s analysis of the racialized zombie to the often-related character of the monster hunter. Exploring figures from The Walking Dead (2010–2022), Weapons (2025), and The Conjuring universe of films, this essay traces the rise of the white male monster hunter and its potential relationship to structural discourses of racism and antiblackness.
